opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be here.

Honestly, it was a pretty gradual shift rather than one big moment. I started out studying business and finance, and the parts I enjoyed most were always the quantitative ones: modeling, working with data, trying to find structure in noisy information. Over time I noticed I was more excited about the tools than about the financial questions themselves.

Around then, language models were starting to do really surprising things. Seeing models pick up skills nobody had explicitly programmed into them felt like one of the most interesting problems I could work on. In finance you're often optimizing something fairly narrow, while AI felt like it could have a much broader impact on science, on how people access information, on almost everything.

So I started teaching myself: online courses, reading papers, and then contributing to open-source projects. That last part was really important. The open research community, with places like Hugging Face and the collaborative efforts around open models, made it possible for someone without a traditional computer science background to get involved and do meaningful work. Once I was actually training models, building benchmarks, and seeing my work get used by other people, it was clear this was what I wanted to spend my time on.

Looking back, the business background has actually helped. It makes you think about what's useful and how things get adopted in the real world, not just what's technically interesting. But the decision itself came down to curiosity. AI research was the thing I kept wanting to do even when nobody was asking me to.

r001.rationale: The response says AI seemed to have broad impact and that curiosity drew him to research, but it does not state that he believed AI would probably be the most important paradigm of his time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I actually started out studying business in undergrad, and I did internships in consulting and finance, that kind of track. And I think what I realized fairly quickly was that a lot of that work felt very incremental to me. You're optimizing something at the margins, and the ceiling on how much impact you can have felt pretty limited.

Around the same time I got exposed to machine learning, partly just out of curiosity, taking some courses and reading papers on the side. And I remember the feeling was very different. It felt like a field where the fundamentals were still being figured out, where a small group of people, or even one person with a good idea, could actually move things. That was really compelling to me.

So I started teaching myself, doing projects, and eventually I got involved in open research efforts, things like BigScience and the BLOOM work, where you could just show up and contribute even without a traditional background. That was a huge deal for me, because I didn't come in through the standard PhD pipeline at first. The openness of the community made the transition possible.

And honestly, I think the business background hasn't been wasted. It made me think a lot about what's actually useful, what people will actually use, and how to prioritize when there are a thousand things you could be working on. That mindset has shaped a lot of the work I've done since, especially around open models and evaluation.

r001.rationale: The response says machine learning felt compelling because its fundamentals were still being figured out and individuals could make an impact. It does not communicate the belief that AI would probably be the most important paradigm of his time.

astra-6.text: For me, it was a gradual shift. I was interested in business and finance, but as I got more exposure to programming and machine learning, I found myself much more drawn to the technical side. I wanted to understand how these systems worked and build things myself. AI research offered that combination of learning, experimenting, and working on problems with potentially broad impact. Eventually, I realized that was what I wanted to spend my time on.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it was realizing that I was more interested in the technology behind a business than in analyzing the business itself. In finance, you spend a lot of time looking at what companies are doing. I found myself wanting to build things instead. AI felt like a field where I could combine that curiosity with programming and work on problems that could have a broad impact. So I started spending more time learning and experimenting, and gradually that became the direction I wanted to pursue.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he preferred building technology and saw AI as a field with broad impact, but does not identify a belief that AI would probably be the most important paradigm of his time.
